description: We are curious minds and creative thinkers united by one mission: turning bold ideas into real-world solutions. We explore NASA's open data, AI, and emerging technologies to create meaningful innovations for Earth. We welcome developers, researchers, data scientists, and problem-solvers who want to push boundaries and build something extraordinary together!
summary:
Every spring, a farmer makes a bet that costs a whole season: which crop goes where. The rain they remember, the frost they expect, the water they count on, all of it has already shifted.

GeoScope lets that farmer play the season out before it happens. Mark a field, set what matters most (water, income, soil, risk), and GeoScope replays every crop rotation through 15 real weather years, built from 35 years of daily NASA POWER data and the open FAO-56 method. No black box, no AI guesswork: every number can be traced and reproduced.

In Jizzakh, Uzbekistan, the winning rotation, wheat–chickpea–sorghum, needs 30 % less irrigation water than cotton–wheat and comes first in 14 of 15 weather years. We show the price too: 33 % less gross income. GeoScope never hides the trade-off. It makes it visible, so the farmer can choose.

Next stop: a field pilot with agronomists.

Test the season before you plant it.
details:
What it does and how it works. GeoScope is a decision-support prototype for irrigated farms. The farmer marks a field on a map, confirms a short “field passport” (soil class, irrigation method, current rotation) and sets priorities: water, income, soil, climate risk. GeoScope then pulls 35 years of daily NASA POWER data (1991 to yesterday: temperature, rain, humidity, wind, solar radiation), computes reference evapotranspiration with the FAO-56 Penman–Monteith method, runs a daily root-zone water balance for every crop, and replays each candidate rotation through every weather year from 2011 to 2025. The result is a ranked comparison of rotations: irrigation need, gross income and climate risk, each shown as a P10 / P50 / P90 range for a wet, a median and a hard year.

Benefits. The farmer tests a rotation before planting instead of guessing. Every number is traceable to open data and an open method; there is no black box, no AI inside the product and no sign-in. If a data source fails, the site says so instead of inventing numbers. The interface works in English and Uzbek, and demo points run offline.

Expected impact. In our Jizzakh, Uzbekistan case study, wheat–chickpea–sorghum needs 30 % less modelled irrigation water than cotton–wheat (−2,788 m³/ha per year) and ranks first in 14 of 15 weather years; the leader does not change when each crop price moves ±20 %. The cost is shown openly: 33 % less gross income. Switching the current rotation from furrow to drip lowers modelled need by a further 3,112 m³/ha. These are modelled results; a pilot with agronomists, comparing model output with recorded irrigation, is our next step.

Tools and technology. Python and FastAPI backend served with Uvicorn; static HTML/JavaScript frontend with Leaflet (maps) and Chart.js (charts); pytest with 22 automated tests, including two FAO-56 worked examples (our ET₀ gives 3.88 mm/day against the published 3.9). Data: NASA POWER (NASA LaRC), NASA GIBS map layers, Open-Meteo forecast, ISRIC SoilGrids. Statistics: linear regression and the Mann–Kendall trend test. No special hardware: it runs on a laptop or a single small server. AI assistants helped write code, text and this submission; AI-generated images are labelled.

Creativity. Most tools give one number for one season. GeoScope replays the future as 15 possible pasts, so every rotation is a range, not a promise. The farmer sets the weights, so the same data gives a different answer for a different farm. And the tool is honest about trade-offs: it shows the water saved and the income given up side by side.

Factors we considered. Uncertainty (weather years, P10–P90, ±20 % prices). The 50 km climate grid, so neighbouring fields share one climate signal. Reanalysis is not a weather station: the temperature trend is significant, but reference evapotranspiration shows no trend, so crop choice drives water need. Income is gross, before costs, from draft reference prices. Not modelled yet: salinity, canal limits, groundwater. GeoScope supports a decision; it does not replace an agronomist.
